Series::LinearAlgAccessor::gen_eigh¶

Back to Series::LinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

template <class ApplyA, class ApplyB, class SolveA>
GenEigResult Series::LinearAlgAccessor::gen_eigh(
    ApplyA&& apply_a,
    ApplyB&& apply_b,
    SolveA&& solve_a,
    const GenEigOptions& options = {}) const

template <class ApplyA, class ApplyB, class SolveA>
GenEigResult SeriesLinearAlgProxy::gen_eigh(
    ApplyA&& apply_a,
    ApplyB&& apply_b,
    SolveA&& solve_a,
    const GenEigOptions& options = {}) const

The Problem It Solves¶

gen_eigh() finds the lowest positive eigenpairs of the generalized Hermitian problem

A x = lambda B x

without requiring either operator to exist as a dense matrix. The receiver is an initial block of trial vectors. Three callables describe how to apply A, apply B, and solve a system with A. This division is useful when a matrix is too large to assemble, when its action is naturally expressed as gathers, stencils, transforms, or scatter-adds, or when a caller already owns a sparse or preconditioned solve.

The method uses zero-shift block inverse iteration. Applying solve_a after apply_b forms the transformed action A^-1 B; its largest transformed eigenvalues are the reciprocals of the generalized eigenvalues nearest zero. Each iteration performs an A-orthonormalization and a small Rayleigh–Ritz solve inside the requested trial subspace. The returned values are therefore ordered from the smallest positive lambda upward.

This is not a dense alternative spelling of eigh(). eigh() owns one materialized square matrix and returns its complete spectrum. gen_eigh() owns no matrix, can request fewer modes than the state dimension, and delegates the expensive operator and inverse actions to the caller.

The Receiver Is A Trial Block¶

The receiver has shape

[..., mode, state]

Each row along mode is one trial vector. The number of rows determines how many eigenpairs are requested; there is no separate count option. Leading dimensions are independent batch dimensions, and every callback must preserve the receiver’s complete shape, dtype, and platform.

The trial rows need not already be normalized or mutually orthogonal. They must be linearly independent in the A inner product and must contain a component in every eigendirection being requested. A zero row, duplicate row, or another rank-deficient block is rejected. A deterministic, problem-informed seed often converges faster than random noise and makes repeated runs reproducible.

mode must be positive and cannot exceed state. A full block with mode == state spans the complete state space; with exact callbacks, its first Rayleigh–Ritz projection can recover the full positive spectrum. A smaller block iterates toward the lowest modes and ordinarily needs more than one outer iteration.

Callback Contracts¶

All three callables receive a const Series& shaped exactly like the trial block and return a Series with that same shape, dtype, and platform. Strides need not match; a callback may return a contiguous result or a valid view.

callback

Required action

Important requirement

apply_a(x)

Return A x for every trial row and batch lane

A must be Hermitian and positive definite on the active state space

apply_b(x)

Return B x for every trial row and batch lane

B must be Hermitian; returned modes must have positive x^H B x

solve_a(rhs)

Return the solution of A y = rhs

Accuracy controls outer convergence; shape, dtype, and platform cannot change

For dense matrices, trial vectors are rows while ordinary matrix multiplication acts on columns. Transpose the block before and after applying or solving the matrix, as Example 2 shows. Matrix-free callables can usually operate on the last state axis directly and avoid those transposes.

solve_a may use a direct factorization, an iterative Krylov solver, a cached preconditioner, or another exact-enough inverse action. gen_eigh() does not assume how the solve is implemented and does not repeat a solve-specific residual check. An inaccurate inverse is visible through slower convergence or nonconverged returned modes.

Options¶

GenEigOptions controls the outer generalized-eigen iteration.

Field

Meaning

Default

max_iterations

Maximum block inverse/Rayleigh–Ritz updates

64

relative_tolerance

Relative residual multiplier for each eigenpair

1e-8

absolute_tolerance

Absolute floor added to the residual threshold

1e-10

All tolerances must be finite and non-negative, and max_iterations must be positive. A mode is marked converged when

||A x - lambda B x||_2
  <= absolute_tolerance
     + relative_tolerance * max(||A x||_2, |lambda| ||B x||_2)

Exhausting the iteration budget is not an exception. The best Ritz estimates are returned with the corresponding .converged lanes set to false, so a caller can report, retry, or reject them under its own policy.

Return Value¶

GenEigResult contains five public fields.

Field

Shape

Meaning

.values

[..., mode]

Positive generalized eigenvalues in ascending order

.vectors

[..., mode, state]

Eigenvectors stored by row and normalized so x^H B x = 1

.residual

[..., mode]

Euclidean norm of A x - lambda B x after final normalization

.converged

[..., mode]

Boolean acceptance result for each returned pair

.iterations

host std::int64_t

Number of outer updates executed

Unlike eigh(), whose eigenvectors occupy columns, gen_eigh() preserves the row-oriented trial-block layout. This keeps every mode as an independent batch lane for matrix-free operators and iterative solves. Eigenvectors still have the usual sign or complex-phase ambiguity; compare equations, projectors, or magnitudes rather than exact vector entries.

Dtype, Platform, And Batching¶

The trial block may be Float32, Float64, Complex64, or Complex128. .values and .residual are real at the corresponding precision; .vectors retain the trial dtype. Integer and Boolean trials are rejected.

The method itself does not move the large state block between platforms. apply_a, apply_b, and solve_a decide where their work runs and must return to the receiver’s platform. The small mode x mode Hermitian decompositions use the eigh() backend, including its documented CPU bridge when the current platform needs one. This keeps the cost of any bridge proportional to the number of requested modes rather than the full state dimension.

Leading batch dimensions are processed together. The implementation has no host loop over a state, mode, or batch lane; only the outer convergence loop is sequential. Operator callbacks should preserve that batching instead of extracting lanes to host memory.

Differentiation¶

gen_eigh() is composed from differentiable Series operations. Reverse history flows through the executed operator actions, inverse actions, orthonormalizations, and Rayleigh–Ritz solves. Consequently, parameters captured by the callbacks receive sensitivities when those callbacks themselves use differentiable operations.

There are three practical qualifications:

  • A callback that detaches, copies through host scalars, or invokes a solver without a reverse rule breaks the graph at that callback.

  • Eigenvector-dependent objectives require separated eigenvalues and must be invariant to sign or complex phase, just as for eigh().

  • The graph records the iterations that actually ran. Tight tolerances can increase both solve time and reverse-memory use.

Eigenvalue-only objectives are usually the most stable differentiable use.

Example Output Helper¶

The examples use this small projection so meaningful digits and shapes remain visible. It is the same helper used by the permanent reference executable.

void values(const char* label, const pluss::Series& value) {
  std::cout << label << "=[";
  const auto lanes = value.host<double>();
  for (std::size_t index = 0; index < lanes.size(); ++index) {
    if (index) std::cout << ", ";
    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(10) << lanes[index];
  }
  std::cout << "] shape=[";
  for (std::int64_t axis = 0; axis < value.dim(); ++axis) {
    if (axis) std::cout << ", ";
    std::cout << value.size(axis);
  }
  std::cout << "]\n";
}

Examples¶

1. A Complete Diagonal Generalized Spectrum¶

Here A = diag(2, 8) and B = diag(1, 2), so the generalized eigenvalues are 2/1 and 8/2. Two independent trial rows span the complete two-state space.

auto seed = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 1.0}, {1.0, -1.0}});
auto a_diag = pluss::make_series({2.0, 8.0});
auto b_diag = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0});

auto result = seed.linearalg.gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(a_diag); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(b_diag); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) { return rhs.div(a_diag); });

values("values", result.values);
values("residual", result.residual);
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "converged=" << result.converged.all().item<bool>() << "\n"
          << "iterations=" << result.iterations << "\n";

Output¶

values=[2.0000000000, 4.0000000000] shape=[2]
residual=[0.0000000000, 0.0000000000] shape=[2]
converged=true
iterations=1

Common Operator Scaling Preserves The Spectrum¶

Multiplying both operators by the same positive constant does not change lambda. Rank detection is relative to the A-Gram spectrum rather than an absolute unit-scale threshold, so very small but well-scaled physical units do not look singular.

auto tiny_a = a_diag.mul(1e-20);
auto tiny_b = b_diag.mul(1e-20);
auto scaled = seed.linearalg.gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(tiny_a); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(tiny_b); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) { return rhs.div(tiny_a); });

values("values", scaled.values);
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "converged=" << scaled.converged.all().item<bool>() << "\n";
Output¶
values=[2.0000000000, 4.0000000000] shape=[2]
converged=true

2. Dense Matrices As Operator Callbacks¶

Dense storage is valid when the state is small. Because trial vectors are rows, the callbacks transpose to columns for matrix multiplication and transpose the result back. Calling through linearalg() uses the proxy signature and is equivalent to the direct accessor style above.

auto a = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 1.0}, {1.0, 3.0}});
auto result = seed.linearalg().gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) {
      return a.linearalg.mm(x.transpose(-2, -1)).transpose(-2, -1);
    },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x; },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) {
      return a.linearalg.lu_solve(rhs.transpose(-2, -1))
          .transpose(-2, -1);
    });

values("values", result.values);
values("B_norm", result.vectors.square().sum(-1, false));
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "equation="
          << a.linearalg.mm(result.vectors.transpose(-2, -1))
                 .transpose(-2, -1)
                 .allclose(result.vectors.mul(result.values.unsqueeze(-1)),
                           1e-9, 1e-9)
          << "\n";

Output¶

values=[2.3819660113, 4.6180339887] shape=[2]
B_norm=[1.0000000000, 1.0000000000] shape=[2]
equation=true

With B = I, the B norm is the ordinary squared Euclidean norm.

3. Request Only The Lowest Mode¶

One trial row requests one eigenpair. The iteration repeatedly amplifies the eigendirection associated with the smallest eigenvalue.

auto result = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 1.0}}).linearalg.gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) {
      return a.linearalg.mm(x.transpose(-2, -1)).transpose(-2, -1);
    },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x; },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) {
      return a.linearalg.lu_solve(rhs.transpose(-2, -1))
          .transpose(-2, -1);
    });

values("value", result.values);
values("residual", result.residual);
std::cout << "iterations=" << result.iterations << "\n";

Output¶

value=[2.3819660113] shape=[1]
residual=[0.0000000224] shape=[1]
iterations=30

The residual is not expected to print as exact zero for an iterative partial solve; it satisfies the configured mixed tolerance.

4. Batch Independent Operator Families¶

The first leading lane uses A = diag(2, 8) and the second uses A = diag(8, 32). Both share B = diag(1, 2).

auto batch_a =
    pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{2.0, 8.0, 8.0, 32.0}, {2, 2});
auto batch_seed = seed.unsqueeze(0).expand({2, 2, 2}, true);
auto result = batch_seed.linearalg.gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(batch_a.unsqueeze(-2)); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(b_diag); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) {
      return rhs.div(batch_a.unsqueeze(-2));
    });

values("values", result.values);
values("residual", result.residual);
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "all_converged=" << result.converged.all().item<bool>() << "\n";

Output¶

values=[2.0000000000, 4.0000000000, 8.0000000000, 16.0000000000] shape=[2, 2]
residual=[0.0000000000, 0.0000000000, 0.0000000000, 0.0000000000] shape=[2, 2]
all_converged=true

5. Complex Hermitian Operators¶

Complex trial vectors use conjugate inner products internally. This example’s off-diagonal entries are a conjugate pair, so the matrix is Hermitian but not real; a plain transpose in the eigensolver would not satisfy this case. Operator callbacks must preserve the complex dtype.

using C = std::complex<double>;
auto complex_seed = pluss::make_series(
    std::vector<C>{{1, 0}, {1, 0}, {1, 0}, {0, 1}}, {2, 2});
auto complex_a = pluss::make_series(
    std::vector<C>{{3, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}, {3, 0}}, {2, 2});
auto complex_b = pluss::make_series(
    std::vector<C>{{1, 0}, {0, 0}, {0, 0}, {1, 0}}, {2, 2});

auto result = complex_seed.linearalg.gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) {
      return complex_a.linearalg.mm(x.transpose(-2, -1)).transpose(-2, -1);
    },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) {
      return complex_b.linearalg.mm(x.transpose(-2, -1)).transpose(-2, -1);
    },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) {
      return complex_a.linearalg.lu_solve(rhs.transpose(-2, -1))
          .transpose(-2, -1);
    });

values("values", result.values);
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "vectors_dtype=" << result.vectors.dtype().name << "\n"
          << "converged=" << result.converged.all().item<bool>() << "\n";

Output¶

values=[2.0000000000, 4.0000000000] shape=[2]
vectors_dtype=complex128
converged=true

6. Inspect A Deliberately Short Iteration Budget¶

Returning a nonconverged estimate lets an application decide whether to retry with a better seed, tighter inverse solve, or larger budget.

auto trial = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 1.0, 1.0}});
auto a_diag3 = pluss::make_series({2.0, 8.0, 32.0});
pluss::Series::LinearAlgAccessor::GenEigOptions options;
options.max_iterations = 1;
options.relative_tolerance = 1e-14;
options.absolute_tolerance = 0.0;

auto result = trial.linearalg.gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(a_diag3); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x; },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) { return rhs.div(a_diag3); }, options);

values("estimate", result.values);
values("residual", result.residual);
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "converged=" << result.converged.all().item<bool>() << "\n"
          << "iterations=" << result.iterations << "\n";

Output¶

estimate=[2.4615384615] shape=[1]
residual=[2.2789417841] shape=[1]
converged=false
iterations=1

7. Differentiate Through Captured Operator Parameters¶

The sum is A[0]/B[0] + A[1]/B[1], so its sensitivity to the two diagonal stiffness values is [1, 1/2].

auto tracked_a = pluss::make_series({2.0, 8.0});
tracked_a.tracks_slope_(true);
auto result = seed.linearalg.gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(tracked_a); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(b_diag); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) { return rhs.div(tracked_a); });

result.values.sum().reverse();
values("values", result.values);
values("d_sum_d_A_diag", tracked_a.sensitivity());
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "has_sensitivity=" << tracked_a.has_sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

values=[2.0000000000, 4.0000000000] shape=[2]
d_sum_d_A_diag=[1.0000000000, 0.5000000000] shape=[2]
has_sensitivity=true

8. Precision Is Preserved¶

auto seed32 = seed.to(pluss::ScalarType::Float32);
auto a32 = a_diag.to(pluss::ScalarType::Float32);
auto b32 = b_diag.to(pluss::ScalarType::Float32);
auto result = seed32.linearalg.gen_eigh(
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(a32); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(b32); },
    [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) { return rhs.div(a32); });

std::cout << "values_dtype=" << result.values.dtype().name << "\n"
          << "vectors_dtype=" << result.vectors.dtype().name << "\n";

Output¶

values_dtype=float32
vectors_dtype=float32

9. Rank, Layout, And Positive-Spectrum Failures¶

try {
  (void)pluss::make_series({{1.0, 0.0}, {2.0, 0.0}})
      .linearalg.gen_eigh(
          [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(a_diag); },
          [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x; },
          [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) { return rhs.div(a_diag); });
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << std::string(e.what()).substr(0, std::string(e.what()).find('\n')) << "\n";
}

try {
  (void)seed.linearalg.gen_eigh(
      [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.select(-1, 0); },
      [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x; },
      [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) { return rhs.div(a_diag); });
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << std::string(e.what()).substr(0, std::string(e.what()).find('\n')) << "\n";
}

try {
  auto negative_b = pluss::make_series({-1.0, -1.0});
  (void)seed.linearalg.gen_eigh(
      [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(a_diag); },
      [&](const pluss::Series& x) { return x.mul(negative_b); },
      [&](const pluss::Series& rhs) { return rhs.div(a_diag); });
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << std::string(e.what()).substr(0, std::string(e.what()).find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

linearalg::gen_eigh: the trial subspace is rank deficient
linearalg::gen_eigh: apply_a must preserve shape, dtype, and platform
linearalg::gen_eigh: requested modes are not in the positive generalized eigenspace

Failure Modes¶

The call rejects an undefined, empty, integral, Boolean, rank-zero, or rank-one trial; mode > state; non-finite trial or callback output; invalid options; rank loss under A; callback shape/dtype/platform drift; a non-positive requested Ritz value; or a non-positive final B norm.

The method cannot prove that opaque callbacks are linear, Hermitian, mutually consistent, or that solve_a actually inverts apply_a. Violating those mathematical contracts can produce nonconvergence or meaningless Ritz pairs without a structural callback error. Verify returned residuals and convergence instead of accepting values solely because the call returned.

Performance Guidance¶

  • Keep state operations matrix-free when possible; only mode x mode projected matrices are materialized.

  • Request only the modes the algorithm consumes. The projected decomposition and block storage grow with mode.

  • Batch independent parameter cases in leading axes rather than calling the method in a host loop.

  • Reuse factorizations or preconditioners inside solve_a; it is called once per outer iteration.

  • Better trial vectors and inverse solves reduce outer iterations. Always read .residual and .converged when using an approximate inverse.
